catalog_quote: Stress is marked by an accent over the vowel; on long vowels the accent is placed over the second member of the pair. Although there are exceptions to the rule, stress generally occurs on the penultimate syllable of Arikara words. [Section 'Isolation versus Discourse Forms', rule (1)] A word ending in a glottal stop in its isolation form will, when another word immediately follows it, lose the glottal stop; at the same time stress shifts from the vowel of the penultimate syllable to the final vowel, which is generally lengthened in slow speech. For example: ISOLATION FORM wiitáʾuʾ 'twenty' / CONNECTED DISCOURSE FORM witaʾú na áxkUx 'twenty-one'; atíkaʾ 'my grandmother' / atiká títka 'my grandmother is sleeping' [Parks et al. 1979: 14] Every word in Arikara, except verb stems, has a stressed syllable. [1979: 74] 6. From these few samples you have learned that: a. When some words are used alone or at the end of a sentence: the final sound is a glottal stop; the last vowel sound, just before the glottal stop, is short; and stress is on the next to last syllable. b. When these same words are used immediately before another word, these changes take place: the glottal stop is dropped, the short vowel sound becomes a long vowel sound; and stress shifts from next to last to the last syllable. [1979: 282] Class III does not take a suffix, but the stress changes from the last syllable in the independent form to the next to the last syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the isolation (citation) form of a word, stress falls on the penultimate syllable, with acknowledged exceptions. Parks's 1979 textbook agrees and adds that every word except a bare verb stem carries one stressed syllable, that stress is marked lexically on every vocabulary item rather than derived by a general rule, and that in connected speech a word followed by another word loses its final glottal stop, lengthens its final vowel and moves stress from the penult to the final syllable (Parks et al. 1979: 74); certain (Class III) verbs mark the subordinate form solely by moving stress from the final to the penultimate syllable (1979: 282).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. The AISRI sound key labels the acute as 'primary stress' but no secondary stress is marked or discussed in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Parks: 'Although there are exceptions to the rule' (unspecified). Parks et al. 1979: verb stems are unstressed (p.14, p.~112); independent verb forms may bear final stress, shifting to the penult in the subordinate form (p.282); the connected-discourse shift to final stress applies to words ending in a glottal stop and also to words ending in a short vowel without glottal stop (p.74). Devoicing (whispering) is restricted to unstressed syllables (1979: 14-15).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, stated for the isolation form in which text words are transcribed; connected-discourse (phrase-medial) forms shift stress to the final syllable. The source is the phonology/orthography section of the compilers introduction to a text collection (the print original is the Introduction to Parks 1991 vol. 1), not a stand-alone grammar; the 1979 work is a pedagogical grammar. Both are by the principal Arikara specialist and are first-hand.
new_statements.identity_note: Arikara proper (arik1262, ISO ari), Fort Berthold Reservation, ND; the AISRI texts (recorded 1970-1988) and the 1979 textbook (White Shield community) describe the same late-20th-century variety. No dialect division is invoked by either source.

sources.note: Section 'Orthography': stress marked by an acute accent (on the second member of a long vowel); 'Although there are exceptions to the rule, stress generally occurs on the penultimate syllable of Arikara words.' Section 'Isolation versus Discourse Forms', rule (1): a word ending in a glottal stop loses it before a following word and stress shifts from the penultimate vowel to the final vowel, which is generally lengthened (wiitáʾuʾ 'twenty' ~ witaʾú na áxkUx 'twenty-one'; atíkaʾ ~ atiká títka).
